Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette: Akua had always taken pride in her role as a judge, known for her fairness and composed demeanor. But it was a façade that began to crumble after the torture she endured during a kidnapping ordeal while on a diplomatic mission abroad five years ago. The memories of those three days were fragmented and elusive, but certain sensory details could transport her back to that dingy, cramped space with unsettling ease. Heavy breathing sounds, like the labored gasps of her captors as they pinned her down, made Akua's skin crawl. Even in the courtroom, when an anxious witness or defendant would inhale deeply before speaking, she'd feel a jolt of anxiety, her mind racing back to that helpless state. The smell of a specific perfume or cologne, one that her tormentor had worn, could catch her off guard at any moment - on the street, in a meeting, or even in her own home - and send her spiraling into a vortex of fear. As she tried to make sense of those traumatic events, Akua found herself struggling to recall specific details deliberately. It was as if her mind had built a barrier around the memories, refusing to let them resurface. When she attempted to force the recollections, she'd experience a strange disconnection - the memories felt like they belonged to someone else, not her. There were even parts of the ordeal that remained stubbornly shrouded in darkness, inaccessible no matter how hard she tried. But it was precisely these elusive memories that seemed to fuel the triggers that haunted her. When Akua caught a whiff of that perfume or heard the sound of heavy breathing, it was as if the memories - hazy and indistinct though they were - would rise up from the depths of her mind, taunting her with their inaccessibility. The more she tried to push them away, the more they seemed to seep into her daily life, contaminating even the most mundane moments. As a judge, Akua prided herself on her ability to remain impartial and composed under pressure. But as time went by, it became increasingly difficult for her to maintain that professional façade. The triggers were relentless, and with each passing day, she felt herself becoming more isolated, more withdrawn. It was as if the memories - fragmented and alien though they seemed - had developed a malevolent life of their own, feeding on her fear and anxiety. It was only when Akua found herself withdrawing from her husband and children, unable to explain why she couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly "on edge," that she realized she needed help. She was tired of living in a state of suspended animation, trapped between the memories she couldn't access and the triggers that seemed to haunt her every waking moment. With a deep sense of trepidation, Akua made the decision to seek therapy, hoping against hope that it might provide her with a way out of this endless cycle of fear and avoidance.
